title: Apparent Zero-Momentum Signals from Magnon--Magnon Interference in Near-Field Spin-Wave Imaging
authors: Julien Berthomier, Romain Lebrun, Vincent Cros, Jamal Ben Youssef, Karim Bouzehouane, Abdelmadjid Anane
abstract: Spatially resolved measurements of coherent waves are commonly read as direct maps of the underlying eigenmode spectrum. We show that this interpretation fails in near-field imaging of multimode spin-wave transport. Scanning nitrogen-vacancy magnetometry of yttrium iron garnet reveals pronounced apparent low-wave-vector signals at frequencies for which no propagating spin-wave mode exists. By tuning the probe-sample distance and modeling the anisotropic near-field response, we identify their origin as coherent mixing between directly excited Damon-Eshbach waves and defect- or transducer-scattered spin waves: the measured signal acquires spatial Fourier components at the difference wave vector $\mathbf{k}_{\mathrm{exc}}-\mathbf{k}_{\mathrm{scat}}$, which can vanish even though both constituent waves carry finite momentum. These results establish that near-field spectra of coherent excitations are interferometric field spectra rather than eigenmode maps, providing both a caution and a framework for identifying scattering processes in nanoscale magnonic devices.
summary: This work demonstrates that near-field imaging of spin waves does not provide a direct map of the material's eigenmodes. By analyzing the interference between different spin-wave components, the authors show that apparent zero-momentum signals are artifacts of magnon-magnon interference, providing a necessary framework for interpreting complex wave measurements in magnonics.
main_problem: The standard interpretation that spatially resolved measurements of coherent waves directly map the underlying eigenmode spectrum fails in near-field imaging of multimode spin-wave transport.
main_result: The observed low-momentum signals are not due to true propagating modes but arise from coherent magnon-magnon interference between directly excited and scattered spin waves.
method: The study combines scanning nitrogen-vacancy (NV) magnetometry experiments with advanced theoretical modeling, including the Near-Field Diffraction (NFD) framework and Biot-Savart law calculations.
model_or_system: The system is spin-wave transport in a yttrium iron garnet (YIG) film, probed by a local, phase-coherent microwave-field sensor (NV magnetometry). The signal is modeled as the superposition of multiple interfering magnetic fields.
key_observables: The measured signal's spatial Fourier components, particularly the anomalous components appearing near zero wave vector ($\mathbf{k} \approx 0$).
important_parameters: Probe-sample distance ($d$), excitation wave vectors ($\mathbf{k}_{	ext{exc}}$) and scattering wave vectors ($\mathbf{k}_{	ext{scat}}$), and the difference wave vector $\Delta\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{k}_{	ext{exc}} - \mathbf{k}_{	ext{scat}}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the measured signal is proportional to the local microwave power and utilizes the quasi-magnetostatic approximation for field calculations.
figures_summary: Figures show experimental contrast at varying probe distances, FFTs revealing anomalous low-k components, and simulations confirming these components originate from the cross-term interference.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the failure of the direct eigenmode mapping assumption, then models the total field as a sum of interfering components, and finally uses simulations and experiments to isolate the interference term as the source of apparent zero-momentum signals.
why_interesting: The concept of interpreting measured fields as interferometric spectra rather than intrinsic mode spectra is crucial for understanding wave phenomena in nanoscale devices, which has parallels in quantum optics and condensed matter wave physics.
